---
title: "2. Hill numbers, completeness and coverage"
description: "What diversity is, why Hill numbers are the standard, how complete your sampling is, and how to estimate the diversity you did not see."
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  dev.args = list(bg = "white"),
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", out.width = "100%",
  dpi = 150, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5
)
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(tidydiversity)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
ants <- filter(png_ants, season == "wet")
```

The data are ant records at baits in the wet season at five elevations on
Mt Wilhelm, Papua New Guinea (200 to 2,200 m). Each row is one species at
one bait. To keep the theory simple, this chapter treats every record as
one observation (as for abundance data, $n$ = number of records). For a
formal incidence analysis, with baits as sampling units, give
`unit = bait` (Chapter 1); the logic and the reading of the results are
the same.

## 1. What is diversity? Hill numbers

### The concept

Diversity combines two things: **how many** species there are
(richness) and **how evenly** individuals are spread among them. A forest
with 10 species, one making up 91 % of the trees, feels less diverse than
one with 10 equally common species. Classic indices (Shannon *H′*,
Simpson *D*) capture this but are on incompatible scales: doubling the
species does not double *H′*.

**Hill numbers** (Hill 1973) solve this. The Hill number of order $q$ is

$$
^{q}D = \left( \sum_{i=1}^{S} p_i^{\,q} \right)^{1/(1-q)}
$$

where $p_i$ is the relative abundance of species $i$ and $S$ the number of
species. It is the **effective number of species**: the number of
*equally common* species that would give the same diversity. All Hill
numbers are in units of species, and a community with twice as many
equally common species has exactly twice the diversity (the "replication
principle"; Jost 2006; Chao et al. 2014).

| Order | Formula | Equals | Sensitive to | Read it as |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $q = 0$ | $S$ | Species richness | Rare species as much as common ones | Number of species |
| $q = 1$ | $\exp(H')$ | Exponential of Shannon entropy | Species in proportion to abundance | Number of "typical" species |
| $q = 2$ | $1 / \sum p_i^2$ | Inverse Simpson index | Common species | Number of dominant species |

Reading them together describes **evenness**: if $^0D$, $^1D$ and $^2D$ are
similar, the community is even; if they fall steeply with $q$, a few
species dominate.

```{r hill}
obs <- div_hill(ants, q = 0:2)
knitr::kable(tidyr::pivot_wider(obs, names_from = q, names_prefix = "q", values_from = diversity),
  digits = 1, caption = "Observed Hill numbers per site (n = number of records)."
)
```

**Interpretation.** At `r obs$site[1]` there are
`r obs$diversity[obs$site == obs$site[1] & obs$q == 0]` species but only
`r round(obs$diversity[obs$site == obs$site[1] & obs$q == 2], 1)` effective
dominant ones: a few species occupy most baits. The steep fall from
$q = 0$ to $q = 2$ is a signature of unevenness.

### Diversity profiles

Plotting $^qD$ continuously from $q = 0$ to $q = 2$ shows the whole picture
at once. Curves that cross mean the ranking of sites depends on whether
you weight rare or common species, which is itself a result worth
reporting.

```{r profile, fig.alt = "Diversity profiles of ants at five elevations, from q = 0 to q = 2"}
prof <- div_hill(ants, q = seq(0, 2, by = 0.1))
ggplot(prof, aes(q, diversity, colour = site)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_tidydiversity() +
  labs(x = "Order q", y = "Effective number of species", colour = NULL) +
  theme_tidydiversity()
```

## 2. How complete is the sample? Coverage

### The concept

No sample contains every species. The question is how much of the
community it **represents**. Turing and Good (Good 1953) showed that the
proportion of the community belonging to species *not yet seen* can be
estimated from the **singletons** ($f_1$, species seen once): if many
species were seen only once, many more are still unseen.

**Sample coverage** is the estimated proportion of individuals in the
community that belong to species present in the sample (Chao and Jost
2012):

$$
\hat{C} = 1 - \frac{f_1}{n} \left[ \frac{(n-1) f_1}{(n-1) f_1 + 2 f_2} \right]
$$

with $n$ the sample size and $f_2$ the number of doubletons. A coverage
of 0.9 means the next individual (or record) sampled has a 10 % chance of
being a species not yet seen.

```{r coverage}
cov <- div_coverage(ants)
knitr::kable(cov, digits = 3,
  caption = "Sample size, observed species, singletons, doubletons and coverage."
)
```

**Interpretation.** Coverage ranges from
`r round(min(cov$coverage), 2)` (`r cov$site[which.min(cov$coverage)]`) to
`r round(max(cov$coverage), 2)` (`r cov$site[which.max(cov$coverage)]`).
`r cov$site[which.min(cov$coverage)]` has the most singletons relative to
its sample: it is the least completely sampled, so its observed richness
underestimates the truth the most. As a rule of thumb:

| Coverage | Sampling is | Observed richness is |
|---|---|---|
| > 0.95 | Nearly complete | Close to the truth |
| 0.80-0.95 | Adequate for most comparisons | An underestimate; compare at equal coverage (Chapter 3) |
| < 0.80 | Incomplete | A clear underestimate; extrapolate or sample more |

### Completeness profiles

Coverage concerns individuals (it is the completeness of order $q = 1$).
**Sample completeness** generalises it to every order (Chao et al. 2020):
for $q = 0$ it is the share of *species* detected; for $q = 2$ the share
weighted towards common species. Completeness is always lowest at $q = 0$,
because rare species are the ones most likely to be missed.

```{r completeness, fig.alt = "Sample completeness profiles from q = 0 to q = 2 for five sites"}
set.seed(1)
comp <- div_completeness(ants, nboot = 50)
ggplot(comp, aes(q, completeness, colour = site, fill = site)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.12, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_tidydiversity() +
  scale_fill_tidydiversity() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Order q", y = "Sample completeness", colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_tidydiversity()
```

**Interpretation.** At $q = 0$ completeness is well below 1 for every site:
many species are still undetected. By $q = 2$ it is close to 1: the
*common* species are well sampled. So conclusions about dominant species
are robust; conclusions about richness are not, unless corrected.

## 3. Estimating true diversity

### The concept

Observed richness depends on how hard you looked. **Asymptotic
estimators** predict the diversity of the whole community (the asymptote
of the species-accumulation curve) from the frequencies of rare species.
For richness this is the **Chao1** estimator (Chao 1984):

$$
\hat{S} = S_{obs} + \frac{n-1}{n} \frac{f_1^2}{2 f_2}
$$

a *lower bound*: the true richness is at least this. Chao et al. (2014)
give corresponding estimators for $q = 1$ and $q = 2$.

```{r estimate}
set.seed(1)
est <- div_estimate(ants, q = 0:2, nboot = 100)
knitr::kable(est, digits = 1,
  caption = "Observed and asymptotic Hill numbers with bootstrap 95 % intervals."
)
```

**How to read it.**

- `estimate` is the predicted diversity of the whole community, with its
  bootstrap standard error and 95 % interval.
- The gap between `observed` and `estimate` is largest at $q = 0$ and
  smallest at $q = 2$, mirroring the completeness profiles.
- Wide intervals for $q = 0$ are normal: estimating how many rare species
  you did *not* see is hard. Treat asymptotic richness as an order of
  magnitude when coverage is low; $q = 1$ and $q = 2$ estimates are much
  more precise and usually the better basis for conclusions.

## How to report it

> We quantified diversity as Hill numbers of order q = 0 (species
> richness), 1 (exponential Shannon) and 2 (inverse Simpson), using
> tidydiversity (Moses 2026) in R. Sample coverage ranged from
> `r round(min(cov$coverage), 2)` to `r round(max(cov$coverage), 2)`
> (Chao and Jost 2012). Asymptotic diversity was estimated following Chao
> et al. (2014), with 95 % confidence intervals from 100 bootstrap
> replicates.
